claim: EPF1 is a founding member of the secreted peptide ligands enforcing stomatal patterning.
source: EPIDERMAL PATTERNING FACTOR1 (EPF1) is a founding member of the secreted peptide ligands enforcing stomatal patterning.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about EPF1.

claim: ERL1 is the primary receptor of EPF1.
source: EPF1 and its primary receptor ERECTA-LIKE1 (ERL1) target MUTE
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by genetic and biochemical studies referenced in the introduction.

claim: EPF1 and ERL1 target MUTE, a transcription factor specifying the proliferation-to-differentiation switch within the stomatal cell lineages.
source: EPF1 and its primary receptor ERECTA-LIKE1 (ERL1) target MUTE, a transcription factor specifying the proliferation-to-differentiation switch within the stomatal cell lineages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in the results section.

claim: MUTE directly induces ERL1.
source: In turn, MUTE directly induces ERL1.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP data and qRT-PCR experiments showing MUTE binding to ERL1 promoter.

claim: The absolute co-expression of ERL1 and MUTE, with the co-presence of EPF1, triggers autocrine inhibition of stomatal fate.
source: The absolute co-expression of ERL1 and MUTE, with the co-presence of EPF1, triggers autocrine inhibition of stomatal fate.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through genetic experiments with MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP.

claim: During normal stomatal development, autocrine inhibition prevents extra symmetric divisions of stomatal precursors likely owing to excessive MUTE activity.
source: During normal stomatal development, this autocrine inhibition prevents extra symmetric divisions of stomatal precursors likely owing to excessive MUTE activity.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by time-lapse imaging data showing extra symmetric divisions in tmm mutants.

claim: ERL1-YFP is localized sharply at the plasma membrane in early stomatal-lineage cells.
source: In early stomatal-lineage cells, including rectangular MMCs and early meristemoids, ERL1-YFP is localized sharply at the plasma membrane (Figure 1A–C,K,L; Video 1).
evidence: Directly observed through confocal microscopy imaging of ERL1pro::ERL1-YFP.

claim: ERL1-YFP exhibits striking accumulation at the newly-formed division site during asymmetric divisions of stomatal-lineage cells.
source: During the asymmetric divisions of stomatal-lineage cells, ERL1-YFP exhibited striking accumulation at the newly-formed division site that separates the meristemoid and stomatal lineage ground cell (SLGC) (Figure 1D,F,M; Video 1).
evidence: Directly observed through time-lapse confocal microscopy imaging.

claim: ERL1-YFP shows transient yet high accumulation during the late meristemoid-to-GMC transition.
source: During the late meristemoid-to-GMC transition, ERL1-YFP showed transient yet high accumulation in the meristemoids while diminishing from the stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs), marking the late meristemoids the brightest (Figure 1G,H,N,O; Video 1).
evidence: Directly observed through time-lapse confocal microscopy imaging.

claim: Expression of ERL1 disappears as the GMC divides symmetrically and differentiates into guard cells.
source: Expression of ERL1 disappears as the GMC divides symmetrically and differentiates into guard cells (Figure 1J,P,Q; Video 1).
evidence: Directly observed through time-lapse confocal microscopy imaging.

claim: ERL1 is a high-confidence SPCH target gene.
source: It has been reported that ERL1 is a high-confidence SPCH target gene (Lau et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: All late meristemoids co-expressed MUTE-tagRFP in the nuclei and strong ERL1-YFP at the cell periphery.
source: However, all late meristemoids co-expressed MUTE-tagRFP in the nuclei and strong ERL1-YFP at the cell periphery (n = 270; 12 seedlings analyzed) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of dual reporter lines showing co-expression in 270 cells.

claim: iMUTE triggered rapid upregulation in ERL1 transcripts within two hours.
source: iMUTE triggered rapid upregulation in ERL1 transcripts also within two hours, indicating that ERL1 is an early MUTE-induced gene (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR analysis following estradiol-inducible MUTE overexpression.

claim: MUTE binds to the ERL1 promoter region overlapping with the known SPCH binding site.
source: A robust binding of MUTE was detected within the ERL1 promoter at the region overlapping with the known SPCH binding site (Lau et al., 2014), which contains the predicted bHLH-binding E-box (Figure 2H,I; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B,D).
evidence: Demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments using MUTE-GFP.

claim: The onset of MUTE expression precedes that of EPF1.
source: A population of meristemoids only exhibited nuclear RFP signals, suggesting that the onset of MUTE expression precedes that of EPF1 (14/180 cells expressed RFP only; from five seedlings) (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Observed through dual reporter analysis showing sequential expression patterns.

claim: MUTE and EPF1 are co-expressed in late meristemoids and GMCs.
source: In the late meristemoids and GMCs, strong RFP and GFP signals co-exist, indicating that MUTE and EPF1 are co-expressed (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Observed through dual reporter analysis.

claim: iMUTE induction did not trigger any substantial changes in EPF1 expression.
source: Unlike ERL1, however, iMUTE induction did not trigger any substantial changes in EPF1 expression (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), suggesting that EPF1 is not likely a MUTE target.
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR analysis following MUTE overexpression.

claim: EPF1 overexpression or exogenous EPF1 peptide application confers arrested meristemoids in ERL1-dependent manner.
source: EPF1 overexpression or exogenous EPF1 peptide application confers arrested meristemoids, a phenotype resembling mute, in ERL1-dependent manner (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: iEPF1 conferred a loss of signals from both MUTE transcriptional and translational reporters 4 days after induction.
source: iEPF1 conferred a loss of signals from both MUTE transcriptional (MUTEpro::nucYFP) and translational (MUTEpro::MUTE-GFP) reporters 4 days after induction when arrested meristemoid phenotypes are evident (Figure 3A).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy of reporter lines following EPF1 overexpression.

claim: Signals for SCRM transcriptional and translational reporters remained in arrested meristemoids even after 4 days of iEPF1.
source: By contrast, signals for SCRM transcriptional (SCRMpro::nucGFP) and translational (SCRMpro::GFP-SCRM) reporters remained in arrested meristemoids even after 4 days (Figure 3B).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy of reporter lines following EPF1 overexpression.

claim: The MUTE-GFP signals started to diminish at 15 hr after the iEPF1 induction and became barely detectable by 20 hr.
source: The MUTE-GFP signals started to diminish at 15 hr after the iEPF1 induction and became barely detectable by 20 hr after the induction. By 24 hr, MUTE-GFP signals were undetectable (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Quantitative time-course analysis of MUTE-GFP fluorescence intensity.

claim: Transcriptional and translational reporters of SCRM were not influenced by iEPF1 within the 24 hr timeframe.
source: Within the same timeframe, transcriptional and translational reporters of SCRM were not influenced by iEPF1 (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Quantitative time-course analysis of SCRM reporter fluorescence intensity.

claim: Strong GFP signals of both SPCHpro::nucGFP and SPCHpro::SPCH-GFP were detected even three days after iEPF1 overexpression.
source: Strong GFP signals of both SPCHpro::nucGFP and SPCHpro::SPCH-GFP were detected even three days after iEPF1 overexpression (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy of reporter lines following EPF1 overexpression.

claim: SPCH transcriptional and translational reporter signals are not changed by iEPF1.
source: Further quantitative analysis of SPCH transcriptional and translational reporters showed that their signals are not changed by iEPF1 (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Quantitative time-course analysis of SPCH reporter fluorescence intensity.

claim: MUTE, but not SPCH, is the specific target of EPF1-mediated signaling.
source: On the basis of these findings, we conclude that MUTE, but not SPCH, is the specific target of EPF1-mediated signaling.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from differential effects of EPF1 on MUTE vs SPCH reporters.

claim: Expression of MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP in er erl1 erl2 conferred massive clusters of arrested meristemoids in the leaf epidermis.
source: Strikingly, the expression of MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP in er erl1 erl2 conferred massive clusters of arrested meristemoids in the leaf epidermis (Figure 5B; Video 3).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy of transgenic lines.

claim: Stomatal index underwent 14-fold reduction from 42.6 ± 5.3% to 2.9 ± 2.1% when MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP was expressed in er erl1 erl2.
source: Consistently, stomatal index (SI=total number of stomata/total number of epidermal cells x100) underwent 14-fold reduction from 42.6 ± 5.3% to 2.9 ± 2.1% (mean ± standard deviation) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of stomatal index from microscopy images.

claim: MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP in er erl1 erl2 epf1 epf2 quintuple mutant background was not able to suppress stomatal differentiation.
source: Indeed, MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP in er erl1 erl2 epf1 epf2 quintuple mutant background was not able to suppress stomatal differentiation, resulting in increased stomatal index (SI) (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis of stomatal index.

claim: Application of bioactive Stomagen peptide to MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP er erl1 erl2 seedlings conferred clusters of mature stomata.
source: By contrast, application of bioactive Stomagen peptide (5 μM) to MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP er erl1 erl2 seedlings conferred clusters of mature stomata (Figure 5G).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy following peptide treatment.

claim: Loss-of-function tmm mutation fully reverted the arrested meristemoid phenotype of MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP in er erl1 erl2.
source: Consistently, loss-of-function tmm mutation fully reverted the arrested meristemoid phenotype of MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP in er erl1 erl2 (Figure 5C, H, I).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy and quantitative analysis of stomatal index.

claim: The co-presence of EPF1, ERL1, and MUTE in the late meristemoids elicits autocrine inhibitory signaling, leading to a termination of stomatal fate.
source: On the basis of these findings, we conclude that the co-presence of EPF1, ERL1, and MUTE in the late meristemoids elicits autocrine inhibitory signaling, leading to a termination of stomatal fate.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic experiments showing arrested meristemoids with MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP and rescue by removing EPF1, Stomagen, or TMM.

claim: Expression of MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP did not confer discernable phenotype in wild-type background with all three ERECTA-family genes.
source: Indeed, the expression of MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP did not confer discernable phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy of transgenic lines in wild-type background.

claim: MUTE-tagRFP signal intensity in each nucleus is substantially higher in tmm, with over 2.5-fold higher average total intensity compared to wild type.
source: As shown in Figure 6A and C, MUTE-tagRFP signal intensity in each nucleus is substantially higher in tmm, with over 2.5-fold higher average total intensity in each nucleus compared to wild type.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity from confocal microscopy images.

claim: The duration of proliferation-to-differentiation transition is significantly shorter in tmm, with averages of 18.9 hr in wild type vs. 14 hr in tmm.
source: Notably, the duration of proliferation-to-differentiation transition (i.e. hours from the last asymmetric division to the onset of symmetric division of a given stomatal precursor cell) is significantly shorter in tmm, with averages of 18.9 hr in wild type (n = 18) vs. 14 hr in tmm (n = 28) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data.

claim: In tmm, meristemoids accumulating high MUTE-tagRFP signals undergo symmetric division, giving rise to two daughter cells both expressing MUTE-tagRFP.
source: Moreover, we observed instances in tmm whereby the meristemoid accumulating high MUTE-tagRFP signals undergoes a symmetric division, giving rise to two daughter cells, both expressing MUTE-tagRFP, and eventually differentiating into paired stomata (Figure 6E, Video 5).
evidence: Observed through time-lapse confocal microscopy imaging.

claim: Loss of the autocrine EPF1-ERL1 signaling causes accelerated and dysregulated stomatal differentiation, likely as a ramification of excessive MUTE accumulation.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that loss of the autocrine EPF1-ERL1 signaling during normal stomatal development causes accelerated and dysregulated stomatal differentiation, likely as a ramification of excessive MUTE accumulation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from time-lapse imaging and quantitative analysis showing shorter transition time and extra symmetric divisions in tmm.

claim: EPF1 peptide is perceived by ERL1/TMM in the meristemoids/GMCs.
source: Here, EPF1 peptide is perceived by ERL1/TMM in the meristemoids/GMCs.
evidence: This is part of the autocrine model proposed in the discussion based on experimental findings.

claim: The pool of EPF1 is shared by both the meristemoid and its neighboring stomatal lineage ground cell (SLGC).
source: Our findings revise these models and propose a buffered system, whereby the pool of EPF1 is shared by both the meristemoid and its neighboring stomatal lineage ground cell (SLGC) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings showing co-expression patterns and genetic interactions.

claim: ERL1 and TMM accumulate at the plasma membrane of stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs), albeit in lesser amounts.
source: ERL1 and TMM also accumulates at the plasma membrane of stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs), albeit in lesser amounts (Figure 1) (Nadeau and Sack, 2002; Horst et al., 2015).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy and cited from previous publications.

claim: ERECTA and ERL2 receptor population expressed in stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs) buffer excessive EPF1 peptide ligands.
source: It is therefore most likely that, in addition to ERL1, ERECTA and ERL2 receptor population expressed in stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs) buffer excessive EPF1 peptide ligands to ensure the proper and adequate level of MUTE inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP causes severe phenotype only when all three ERECTA-family receptors are missing.

claim: YODA, MKK4/5, and MPK3/6 are genetically acting downstream of the three ERECTA-family RKs.
source: First, YODA, MKK4/5, and MPK3/6 are genetically acting downstream of the three ERECTA-family RKs (Lampard et al., 2008; Bemis et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: Expression of constitutively-active MKK4/5 by the MUTE promoter led to arrested meristemoids.
source: Second, the expression of constitutively-active MKK4/5 by the MUTE promoter led to arrested meristemoids (Lampard et al., 2009), thus phenocopying EPF1 peptide application or overexpression (Hara et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: MUTE does not possess a predicted MAP kinase target domain.
source: Unlike SPCH, however, MUTE does not possess a predicted MAP kinase target domain (Davies and Bergmann, 2014), raising a question of whether MUTE is a MPK3/6 substrate.
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: Intrinsic polarity of meristemoids and asymmetric daughter cell fates are regulated by BASL.
source: Intrinsic polarity of meristemoids and asymmetric daughter cell fates are regulated by BASL (Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: Polarized BASL in the stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs) enhances the MAP kinase activity, resulting in lowered SPCH abundance.
source: Recent studies have revealed that polarized BASL in the stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs) enhances the MAP kinase activity, resulting in lowered SPCH abundance (Zhang et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: In the absence of EPF1, GFP-BASL occasionally exhibits improper polar localization to the 'wrong' site within a periphery of the stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs).
source: In the absence of EPF1, GFP-BASL occasionally exhibits improper polar localization to the 'wrong' site within a periphery of the stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs), which predicts the mis-oriented site of asymmetric spacing division (Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: The tomato cysteine-rich secreted protein LAT52 and its receptor LRR-RK, LePRK2, are both expressed in pollen.
source: For instance, the tomato cysteine-rich secreted protein LAT52 and its receptor LRR-RK, LePRK2, are both expressed in pollen (Muschietti et al., 1998; Tang et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: Both CLE45 and BAM3 are expressed in protophloem tissue in roots, and their signal transduction leads to the inhibition of protophloem differentiation.
source: Another example is CLE45-BAM3, a small secreted peptide ligand-LRR-RK pair: both CLE45 and BAM3 are expressed in protophloem tissue in roots, and their signal transduction leads to the inhibition of protophloem differentiation (Depuydt et al., 2013; Rodriguez-Villalon et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: Wnt participates in the autocrine regulation of epidermal stem cell renewal in mice.
source: For instance, Wnt, a key secreted cell-cell signal during animal development (Logan and Nusse, 2004), participates in the autocrine regulation of epidermal stem cell renewal in mice (Lim et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: ERL1pro::ERL1-YFP rescues the stomatal cluster phenotype in er erl1 erl2.
source: This construct rescues the stomatal cluster phenotype in er erl1 erl2, indicating it is functional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic complementation and phenotypic analysis.

claim: The expression level of the ERL1-YFP transgene is comparable to that of the endogenous ERL1.
source: Consistently, the expression level of the ERL1-YFP transgene is comparable to that of the endogenous ERL1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated through RT-PCR analysis.

claim: The transition from meristemoids to GMCs is specified by SPCH's sister bHLH protein, MUTE.
source: The transition from meristemoids to GMCs is specified by SPCH's sister bHLH protein, MUTE (Pillitteri et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: EPF2 is a direct transcriptional target of SPCH and SCRM.
source: Recent studies established that EPF2 is a direct transcriptional target of SPCH and SCRM, therefore EPF2, ERECTA•TMM, and SPCH•SCRM modules constitute a negative feedback loop generating evenly distributed spatial patterns of stomatal initial cells (Lau et al., 2014; Horst et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: The decision of whether or not to enter the stomatal cell-lineage is fine-tuned by the competitive binding of EPF2 and its antagonistic peptide, EPF-LIKE9 (EPFL9), also known as Stomagen, to ERECTA.
source: Furthermore, the decision of whether or not to enter the stomatal cell-lineage is fine-tuned by the competitive binding of EPF2 and its antagonistic peptide, EPF-LIKE9 (EPFL9), also known as Stomagen, to ERECTA (Kondo et al., 2010; Sugano et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: The direct binding of Stomagen to ERECTA leads to the inhibition of receptor activation and signal transduction.
source: Unlike EPF2, the direct binding of Stomagen to ERECTA leads to the inhibition of receptor activation and signal transduction, therefore resulting in excessive stomatal clusters like erecta-family mutants (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: Loss-of-function mutation of EPF1 confers stomatal pairing and clustering.
source: The founding member of EPF/EPFL-family peptides, EPF1, enforces stomatal spacing and its loss-of-function mutation confers stomatal pairing and clustering (Hara et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: Both genetic and biochemical studies have placed ERECTA-LIKE1 (ERL1) and TMM as a receptor module acting downstream of EPF1.
source: Both genetic and biochemical studies have placed ERECTA-LIKE1 (ERL1), a sister receptor of ERECTA, as well as TMM as a receptor module acting downstream of EPF1 (Hara et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: Both EPF1 and ERL1 promoter activities are the highest in the stomatal precursor cells, most notably in the late meristemoids and GMCs.
source: However, both EPF1 and ERL1 promoter activities are the highest in the stomatal precursor cells, most notably in the late meristemoids and GMCs (Shpak et al., 2005; Hara et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: Stomatal development in Arabidopsis occurs through stereotypical cell-state transition events.
source: Stomatal development in Arabidopsis occurs through stereotypical cell-state transition events: a stomatal initial cell on the protoderm called a meristemoid mother cell (MMC) undergoes an asymmetric entry division to give rise to a meristemoid, a transient amplifying cell of the stomatal lineage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about stomatal development cited from multiple sources.

claim: The meristemoid reiterates asymmetric divisions and renews itself, while creating surrounding stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs).
source: The meristemoid reiterates asymmetric divisions and renews itself, while creating surrounding stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about stomatal development.

claim: The meristemoid loses its stem-cell-like property and differentiates into a guard mother cell (GMC).
source: Eventually, the meristemoid loses its stem-cell-like property and differentiates into a guard mother cell (GMC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about stomatal development.

claim: The GMC executes a single round of symmetric division to form paired guard cells (GCs) surrounding a pore.
source: The GMC executes a single round of symmetric division to form paired guard cells (GCs) surrounding a pore, thereby completing stomatal differentiation (Lau and Bergmann, 2012; Pillitteri and Torii, 2012; Han and Torii, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about stomatal development cited from multiple sources.

claim: Cell state transitions during stomatal development are directed by the sequential actions of three basic-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) proteins, SPEECHLESS (SPCH), MUTE, and FAMA.
source: These cell state transitions are directed by the sequential actions of three basic-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) proteins, SPEECHLESS (SPCH), MUTE, and FAMA, which determine the initiation and proliferation, meristemoid-to-GMC transition, and GMC-to-GC differentiation, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about stomatal development.

claim: SPCH, MUTE, and FAMA form heterodimers with the broadly expressed sister bHLH proteins SCREAM (SCRM) and SCRM2.
source: These three bHLH proteins form heterodimers with the broadly expressed sister bHLH proteins SCREAM (SCRM: also known as ICE1) and SCRM2, both of which are absolutely required for the activities of SPCH-MUTE-FAMA (Lau and Bergmann, 2012; Pillitteri and Dong, 2013; Han and Torii, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: EPF2 peptide perception by ERECTA activates downstream intracellular signals mediated by the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAP kinase) cascade.
source: During the initiation of stomatal cell lineages, EPF2 peptide perception by ERECTA activates downstream intracellular signals mediated by the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAP kinase) cascade, which inhibits the entry divisions of MMC by down-regulating SPCH protein (Lampard et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2012, 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: Application of bioactive EPF2 peptide confers an epidermis solely composed of pavement cells, phenotypically identical to loss-of-function spch mutant.
source: As such, application of bioactive EPF2 peptide confers an epidermis solely composed of pavement cells, phenotypically identical to loss-of-function spch mutant (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: The Stomagen peptide associates with ERL1 in planta.
source: The Stomagen peptide also associates with ERL1 in planta (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: TMM forms a heteromer with ERL1 and is required for EPF1-ERL1 mediated signaling.
source: TMM forms a heteromer with ERL1 and is required for EPF1-ERL1 mediated signaling (Hara et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: TMM is required for the asymmetric spacing division of a neighboring stomatal lineage ground cell (SLGC).
source: It is well known that TMM is required for the asymmetric spacing division of a neighboring stomatal lineage ground cell (SLGC) (Nadeau and Sack, 2002; Lau and Bergmann, 2012; Han and Torii, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: A disproportionate balance of receptor pools between meristemoid and neighboring cell evoke the self-inhibition of stomatal fate.
source: Our findings suggest that both a meristemoid and its neighboring cell share the same source of EPF1 signaling peptides, and a disproportionate balance of receptor pools between these two cell types evoke the self-inhibition of stomatal fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that MUTEpro::ERL1-YFP causes phenotype only in er erl1 erl2 background but not in wild-type.

claim: Endogenous autocrine EPF1-ERL1 signaling in the meristemoids prevents excessive MUTE protein accumulation.
source: The result supports the hypothesis that endogenous autocrine EPF1-ERL1 signaling in the meristemoids prevents excessive MUTE protein accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that MUTE levels are higher in tmm mutants.

claim: More cells express MUTE protein in tmm compared to wild-type epidermis.
source: Also, compared to the wild-type epidermis, more cells express MUTE protein in tmm, consistent with the increase in stomatal precursor cells by tmm mutation (Figure 6C).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy of dual reporter lines.

claim: The role of TMM in suppressing the symmetric division of a meristemoid has been overlooked.
source: On the contrary, the role of TMM in suppressing the symmetric division of a meristemoid has been overlooked.
evidence: This is an observation made by the authors based on their findings.

claim: MUTE and ERL1 constitute a negative feedback loop.
source: The key framework is a negative feedback loop between MUTE and ERL1 whereby MUTE directly upregulates ERL1 expression (Figure 2), and in turn, ERL1 mediates EPF1-peptide signaling leading to inhibition of MUTE activity (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: ERL1 is induced by SPCH in earlier stomatal-lineage cells, including MMCs, early meristemoids, and SLGCs.
source: ERL1 is also induced by SPCH in earlier stomatal-lineage cells, including MMCs, early meristemoids, and SLGCs (Figure 1) (Lau et al., 2014).
evidence: Observed through imaging and cited from previous publication.

claim: EPF1 expression is not regulated by MUTE.
source: While EPF1 expression is not regulated by MUTE, EPF1 turns on during meristemoid-to-GMC transition (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through qRT-PCR showing no change in EPF1 upon MUTE induction, and dual reporter analysis showing EPF1 expression timing.

claim: The overlapping expression of EPF1, ERL1, and MUTE during a narrow developmental window in the late meristemoids triggers downregulation of MUTE.
source: Based on these findings, we proposed a coincidence model where the overlapping expression of EPF1, ERL1, and MUTE during a narrow developmental window in the late meristemoids triggers downregulation of MUTE (Figure 7), thereby ensuring timely transition to stomatal differentiation mediated by FAMA.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: EPF/EPFL-family peptides mediate signals both in autocrine and paracrine manners.
source: Therefore, EPF/EPFL-family peptides mediate signals both in autocrine and paracrine manners.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and comparison with other EPF/EPFL peptides.

claim: EPFL9/Stomagen secreted from internal mesophyll tissues is perceived by ERECTA in the protoderm.
source: For example, EPFL9/Stomagen secreted from internal mesophyll tissues is perceived by ERECTA in the protoderm (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: EPFL4 and EPFL6 are inter cell-layer signals between the stem endodermis and phloem to promote inflorescence elongation via ERECTA.
source: EPFL4 and EPFL6 are inter cell-layer signals between the stem endodermis and phloem to promote inflorescence elongation via ERECTA (Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.

claim: EPFL2 peptide promotes leaf serration as a ligand for ERECTA-family.
source: Recently, we have reported that EPFL2 peptide promotes leaf serration as a ligand for ERECTA-family (Tameshige et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous publication by the same group.

claim: ERL2 shows the highest expression at the leaf teeth tips where EPFL2 expression is excluded.
source: Interestingly, EPFL2 and its primary receptor, ERL2, exhibit inverse expression patterns: ERL2 shows the highest expression at the leaf teeth tips where EPFL2 expression is excluded.
evidence: This is from the authors' recent work on EPFL2.

claim: Both epf1 mutation and a dominant-negative ERL1 receptor confer a violation of one-cell spacing rule.
source: Both epf1 mutation and a dominant-negative ERL1 receptor confer a violation of one-cell spacing rule (Hara et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: EPFL4/6 (CHAL/CLL1) interfere with the buffering mechanism and confer stomatal clustering in the stems in the absence of TMM.
source: Moreover, EPFL4/6 (CHAL/CLL1), which normally act as ligands for ERECTA-mediated inflorescence elongation, interfere with this buffering mechanism and confer stomatal clustering in the stems the absence of TMM (Abrash and Bergmann, 2010; Abrash et al., 2011; Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous publications.

claim: VST-family of membrane-associated proteins was reported as a modulator of ERECTA-family signaling, via specifically interacting with ERL2.
source: Very recently, a VST-family of membrane-associated proteins was reported as a modulator of ERECTA-family signaling, via specifically interacting with ERL2 (Ho et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous publication.
